First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{{e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x}{y}]\text{d}y & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{y}[{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{y}{[\frac{{e}^{2x}}{2}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{y}(\frac{{e}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{0}}{2})\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{{e}^{2}-1}{2y}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{{e}^{2}-1}{2y}\,\text{d}y & =\frac{{e}^{2}-1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{y} \\  & ={[\frac{{e}^{2}-1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}-1}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2({e}^{2}-1)}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A,$ where 
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2\}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express our double integral as a repeated integral:      

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{-1}^{1}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{-1}^{1}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{-1}^{1}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{-1}^{1}\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[(\frac{1}{3}+{y}^{2})-(-\frac{1}{3}-{y}^{2})]\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{2}{3}+2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{2}{3}+2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y & ={[\frac{2y}{3}+\frac{2{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(2+{2}^{3}-0) \\  & =\frac{20}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{D}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}A,$ where 
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 3\}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express our double integral as a repeated integral:      

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{2})]}_{0}^{2}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1)-\operatorname{arctan}⁡0)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{\pi }{8}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\pi }{8}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y & =\frac{\pi }{8}(\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}){|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{24}({3}^{3}-{0}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{9\pi }{8}\end{aligned}
$$

                    Evaluating a Double Integral Over a Rectangular Domain
canonical_examples.problem:
Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint \limits_{D} \dfrac y{x^2} \, \textrm d A$, where 
$D=\left\{ (x,y) \: : \:2 \leq x \leq 4,\: 0 \leq y \leq 3\right\}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we express our double integral as a repeated integral:    

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[-\frac{y}{x}]}_{2}^{4}\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(-\frac{y}{4}-(-\frac{y}{2}))\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{y}{4}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{y}{4}\,\text{d}y & ={[\frac{{y}^{2}}{8}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{{3}^{2}}{8}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{8} \\  & =\frac{9}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Changing the Order of Integration
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following equalities are true given that
$D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2, \: 0 \leq y \leq 1 \big\}.$

I. $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} e^{\sqrt{xy}} \,\text{d}A  = \int_{0}^{1}  \int_{0}^{2}e^{\sqrt{xy}}\,  \text{d}y \, \text{d}x$

II. $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} e^{\sqrt{xy}}\,\text{d}A  = \int_{0}^{2}  \int_{0}^{1} e^{\sqrt{xy}}\, \text{d}y\,  \text{d}x$

III. $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} e^{\sqrt{xy}} \,\text{d}A = \int_{0}^{1}  \int_{0}^{2}e^{\sqrt{xy}}\,  \text{d}x \, \text{d}y$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We notice that: 

- the limits for the variable $x$ are from ${\color{blue}0}$ to ${\color{blue}2}$, and

- the limits for the variable $y$ are from ${\color{red}0}$ to ${\color{red}1}.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the region of integration is rectangular, we can simply swap the order of integration. This gives

$$
\iint\limits_{D} e^{\sqrt{xy}} \,\text{d}A  
= \int_{\color{blue}0}^{\color{blue}{2}} \left[ \int_{\color{red}0}^{\color{red}1} e^{\sqrt{xy}}\,\text{d}{\color{red}y} \right] \text{d}{\color{blue}x} .
$$

So, the correct answer is "II and III only".

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
A **repeated integral**, also known as an **iterated integral,** is an integral in which we carry out repeated integration with respect to different variables. An example of a repeated integral is as follows:

$$
\int_0^1\int_0^1 ye^{xy}\,\textrm d x\,\textrm d y
$$

To evaluate this integral, we first integrate with respect to the inner variable $x,$ and then with respect to the outer variable $y$. We can write this more explicitly as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}y{e}^{xy}\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

We now carry out the integration. First, we integrate with respect to $x,$ *treating $y$ as a constant*. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}y{e}^{xy}\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{y{e}^{xy}}{y}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[{e}^{xy}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{y}-{e}^{0}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{y}-1\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{y}-1\,\text{d}y & ={[{e}^{y}-y]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[e-1]-[1-0] \\  & =e-2.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that

$$
\int_0^1\int_0^1 ye^{xy}\,\textrm d x\,\textrm d y = e-2.
$$

tutorials.name: Double Integrals
tutorials.problem:
Consider the surface $z= f(x,y) = 3-x^2-y^2,$ defined over the following rectangle:

$$
R=[0,1] \times [0,1] = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \: 0 \leq y \leq 1 \big\}.
$$

A sketch of our surface and its domain is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14254993/assets/1fdf4668c7e89a9a32ee8e655fe5c80c899a04d25a0f342365560f4d9abdd8fd.png)

 

The **double integral** of $f(x,y)$ over $R,$ denoted

$$
\iint\limits_{R}{ f(x,y) \, \mathrm{d}A},
$$

represents the total *signed* volume bounded between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the planes $x=0, x=1, y=0, y=1.$

It can be shown that the double integral 

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} {{(3-x^2-y^2) \, \mathrm{d}A}},
$$

can be evaluated using the repeated integral 

$$
\displaystyle \int_0^1\int_0^1 (3-x^2-y^2) \, \mathrm{d}  x\,  \mathrm{d}  y.
$$

Notice that we replace $\textrm d A$ with $\textrm d x\,\textrm d y$ when writing our double integral as a repeated integral.

tutorials.name: The Order of Integration for Double Integrals on a Rectangular Domain
tutorials.problem:
Let's once again consider the integral 

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D}{ { (x^2+y^2) \, \mathrm{d}A}}
$$

over the rectangular domain 

$$
D=[0,1] \times [0,1] = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \: 0 \leq y \leq 1 \big\}.
$$

Similar to definite integrals of single-variable functions, this double integral can be defined as the limit of a Riemann sum, as follows:

$$
\iint\limits_{D}{{f\left( {x,y} \right)\, \mathrm{d}A}} = \mathop {\lim }\limits_{n,\,\,m \to \infty } \sum\limits_{j = 1}^n {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^m {f\big( {x_i^*,y_j^*} \big)\,\Delta x_i \Delta y_j} }
$$

Notice that in the above summation, we could have instead summed over the $j$'s first and then the $i$'s, giving

$$
\iint\limits_{D}{{f\left( {x,y} \right)\, \mathrm{d}A}} = \mathop {\lim }\limits_{m,\,\,n \to \infty } \sum\limits_{i = 1}^m {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^n {f\big( {x_i^*,y_j^*} \big)\,\Delta y_j \Delta x_i} },
$$

and this would result in an iterated integral in the reverse order: 

$$
\iint\limits_{D}{{f\left( {x,y} \right)\, \mathrm{d}A}}  
= \int_0^1\int_0^1 f(x,y)\ \mathrm{d}  y\,  \mathrm{d}  x.
$$

 

Regardless of the order in which we carry out the integration, the answer will always be the same!

Moreover, *provided that the region $D$ is rectangular*, we can swap the order of integration. This means that if 

$$
D=[a,b] \times [c,d] = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: a \leq x \leq b, \: c \leq y \leq d \big\},
$$

then

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={\int }_{c}^{d}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,y)\text{ }dx\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{c}^{d}f(x,y)\text{ }dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$
